summary:
Malatya province falls entirely under Turkey's national legal framework. No statute, police directive, court decision or incident specific to Malatya appears in the sources consulted, so the position of a trans visitor in the province is the position the central authorities have constructed nationally.

There is no visa, entry or border rule specific to LGBTQ travellers; the documented exposure points lie inside the country rather than at the frontier. The visitor-facing document risk is general: foreigners must carry original photo ID at transit checkpoints in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and warnings of detention for non-compliance. In practice that requirement meets street-level identity checks. In August 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women while they were walking, shopping or sitting in cafés in Beyoğlu, held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station and released them after "General Information Gathering" background checks. Legal experts quoted by bianet argue those checks breach Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. Nothing was fined, but names and details were recorded.

Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence in Turkey since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988. No comprehensive law prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and there is no direct discrimination protection for gender identity. Openly LGBTQ people are barred from serving in the military. Same-sex marriage, civil unions, domestic partnerships and joint adoption are not recognised.

The most consequential visitor-facing item is the leaked omnibus "11th Judicial Package", reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025. It would amend penal-code article 225 so that acts "contrary to biological sex and general morality" carry up to three years' imprisonment and same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies up to four years; amend civil-code article 40 ("Changing Sex") to raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from 18 to 25, add a mandatory infertility condition and require evaluation by a government-approved hospital; and imprison care providers for up to seven years and trans patients for up to three years. Amnesty International records that three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025, which would criminalise expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible, but were ultimately not submitted to parliament. Human Rights Watch states criminalisation by statute had not been enacted as of that date, framed as protecting "the family" and "public morals".

The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 records 313 violations over the year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, dominated by 299 detention decisions, 256 taken on the record and 43 off it, alongside systematic attacks on the privacy of LGBT people. Coverage of the same report counts six deaths linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. Hostility at this scale is recorded as state policy rather than residual prejudice.

Policing asymmetry is documented case by case. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy by a 17-year-old; the attacker was released while the victim herself was referred for arrest, which activists describe as evidence of a state hate policy. On 1 December 2025 the transgender prisoner Poyraz was found dead in his cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara. Accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers state that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived after prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison only two days later, and that witness statements were not taken; an opposition MP raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025.

Trans visitors who are detained are held in facilities organised by registered sex rather than gender identity. Turkish prisons subject LGBTI+ detainees to arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto isolation and restricted healthcare; some prisoners refuse hospital transfers for fear of other male inmates. No policy or staff training exists to identify LGBTI+ needs, complaints are ineffective and can provoke further violence, and transfers are frequent.

Public visibility carries its own exposure. Pride parades have been banned by local authorities since 2015, with Istanbul's 2015–2018 parades banned and dispersed. In June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and Trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, and over 90 people were arbitrarily detained; prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through the year, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia. In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling that it had shared "obscene" images incompatible with "society's moral values" that could "encourage or promote" LGBTI identities. In September 2026 police detained dozens in raids on gay bar and the homes of LGBTQ+ activists under a "Decade of Family and Population" crackdown.

Protection machinery is thin. The European Commission's 2025 report found legal protection insufficient and out of line with the EU acquis, while noting official permissions granted to demonstrations promoting exclusion. If medication is needed during a stay, hormone replacement therapy is not covered by the government healthcare system, so trans visitors must obtain and pay for it privately.
tangentialFactors:
Discriminatory framing originates at the top of the state. The Erdoğan government has repeatedly used "the family" and "public morals" to legitimise stigmatisation, and the draft packages sit within a broader authoritarian drift rather than an isolated legislative episode.

Legal trajectory is not uniform. The 12th judicial reform package passed in 2026 dropped provisions discriminating against LGBTQ people and made symbolic same-sex weddings possible, though these carry no legal marital status. In early 2026 Turkish media reported that the government was considering legislation criminalising public advocacy of "behaviour contrary to biological sex", which was not included in that year's package. The direction of travel therefore differs between the reform package and the drafting activity surrounding it.

Turkey's position is measured against a regional benchmark the European Commission uses directly: the EU acquis, against which the 2025 report found the country's protections insufficient.

Document checks are the routine friction point for a foreigner. The general ID-carrying obligation applied to transit checkpoints gives police a lawful pretext for stops, and the August 2025 Taksim episode shows what the follow-on check looks like when the person stopped is a trans woman: no charge, no fine, but a recorded identity and a background check that legal commentators regard as unlawful.

LGBTI+ organising faces judicial and administrative pressure. Local authorities have banned pride parades since 2015; more than 90 people were detained at the banned June 2025 Istanbul marches and prosecutions of 92 participants were still running at the end of that year. Detained residents and prisoners are held according to registered sex, subject to body and strip searches, de facto isolation and restricted healthcare, with frequent transfers and complaints processes that are ineffective and may provoke further violence. outOfScopeNotes:
No province-level source for Malatya was found: no local statute, police practice, court ruling, facility or incident concerning Malatya appears in the inventory. Everything in this record is the national framework applied to the province.

Whether the leaked 11th Judicial Package has been enacted is unresolved. Human Rights Watch reported it on 29 October 2025 as a draft; Amnesty International states that the three draft packages made public during 2025 were ultimately not submitted to parliament; a separate 12th judicial reform package is recorded as having passed in 2026 without the discriminating provisions. The relationship between these legislative items is not settled in the sources.

The scope and outcome of the September 2026 raids under the "Decade of Family and Population" campaign are not sourced beyond the detentions themselves: charges, length of custody and any resulting prosecutions are not documented here.

Regional variation in enforcement across Turkey's provinces is not sourced. Whether Malatya police apply the stops-and-background-checks pattern recorded in Istanbul, or the degree of local hostility relative to Istanbul or İzmir, is not addressed by any source in the inventory.
